strengths: The paper provides a highly systematic and comprehensive exploration of online fair division of indivisible goods across three distinct information regimes: no future information, normalization information, and frequency predictions.

The meta-algorithm (Algorithm 2) is a powerful, elegant, and highly original contribution, proving that any single-shot share-based fairness guarantee (e.g., MMS, RRS, MXS) can be lifted to the online setting under frequency predictions.
The paper identifies and corrects a mistake in a prior work (Kahana and Hazon, 2023) regarding PROP1 allocations, which represents a valuable contribution to the correctness of the literature.
The theoretical bounds presented are exceptionally tight and complete, including a tight approximation ratio of (sqrt(5)-1)/2 for EFX under identical valuations with normalization.
The manuscript is written with exceptional clarity, featuring well-structured proofs, clear definitions, and intuitive explanations.
weaknesses: The frequency predictions model assumes perfect, noiseless predictions of the multiset of future valuations. Exploring the robustness of the meta-algorithm under noisy predictions would significantly enhance its practical applicability.

A significant portion of the positive results for more than two agents are quite weak (e.g., PROP1 under normalization) due to the severe impossibility results established for EF1 and EFX when n >= 3, which somewhat limits the optimistic take of the paper for larger systems.

The setting with identical valuations (Section 6) is highly restricted and its practical applicability to fair division is somewhat limited compared to the heterogeneous case, although it is well-motivated by online scheduling benchmarks.

strengths: The paper provides a comprehensive and highly structured classification of online fair division, exploring multiple information regimes (no information, normalization information, and frequency predictions) and multiple valuation models.

The meta-algorithm in Section 5 (Theorem 5.1) is a very powerful and elegant result, showing that any share-based fairness notion achievable offline can also be achieved online with frequency predictions.
The paper corrects an existing error in prior literature regarding PROP1 guarantees without future information.
The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, with clear definitions, intuitive algorithmic designs, and solid mathematical proofs.
weaknesses: The frequency prediction model assumes perfect/exact frequency predictions of the valuation multisets. In realistic learning-augmented scenarios, these predictions would be noisy, and the paper does not analyze consistency or robustness under imperfect predictions.
Many of the positive results are constrained to the two-agent case ($n=2$), while strong impossibility results (approximation ratio of 0) quickly kick in for $n \ge 3$ across several settings.

strengths: The paper presents a comprehensive and highly systematic study of online fair division under varying degrees of future information, filling important gaps in the literature.

The introduction of the meta-algorithm (Algorithm 2) is a strong, general contribution that elegantly translates any feasible offline share-based guarantee into an online one when frequency predictions are available.
The paper is very well-written, with precise definitions, clear transitions, and detailed proofs for all theoretical claims.
The work identifies and corrects an error in prior work (Kahana and Hazon, 2023) regarding PROP1, which helps clarify the state of the art.
weaknesses: The practical applicability of the algorithms is somewhat limited by the assumption of perfect predictive information (either exact total values or exact frequency multisets). The paper does not analyze the robustness of these guarantees under noisy or erroneous predictions, which is standard in modern learning-augmented algorithms.
The study is restricted to additive valuations. Extending some of the positive results to broader valuation classes (e.g., submodular) remains unaddressed.

There are no experimental evaluations or simulations. While the contributions are primarily theoretical, empirical simulations showcasing average-case performance or the impact of minor prediction errors would have strengthened the paper.

strengths: The paper provides a thorough and systematic map of online fair division across different information regimes, successfully filling several major gaps in the literature.

The meta-algorithm developed for the frequency predictions model (Algorithm 2 and Theorem 5.1) is highly innovative, demonstrating how to lift any offline 'share-based' guarantee to the online setting.

The inclusion of a learning-augmented framework with noisy/imperfect advice is mathematically rigorous, highly relevant for practical ML pipelines, and demonstrates graceful degradation with respect to prediction error.

The manuscript is exceptionally well-written and structured. Table 1 provides an excellent summary of the results, and the intuitive explanations preceding the proofs make the paper highly accessible.
The authors successfully identify and correct a technical error in prior literature (Kahana and Hazon, 2023).
weaknesses: The existence of an EF1 allocation for $n \ge 3$ agents under frequency predictions remains an unresolved open problem (as indicated by the '?' in Table 1), which slightly limits the completeness of the landscape.

The meta-algorithm (Algorithm 2) relies on solving an offline allocation problem to achieve the target share. While this is polynomial-time when the offline share is easy to compute, for several fair-share notions, finding or approximating the share offline can be computationally hard, which inherits as a bottleneck for the online setting.

The paper focuses heavily on a very strong adversarial model (adaptive adversary, ex post evaluation). While theoretically standard, a brief discussion on how the bounds might change under milder stochastic or distributional arrival models would have significantly enhanced the paper's practical relevance to machine learning settings.

strengths: The paper provides a highly comprehensive and systematic mapping of the online fair division landscape under three distinct regimes of future information: no information, normalization information, and frequency predictions.

The general meta-algorithm (Theorem 5.1) for frequency predictions is a powerful and elegant contribution. It successfully bridges offline 'share-based' guarantees with the online setting, showing that any feasible offline share can be matched online (e.g., yielding the best-known SODA'24 MMS approximation online).

The authors appropriately address the practical realities of machine-learned predictions by providing robust learning-augmented analyses (noisy normalization in Section 4.1 and noisy frequency predictions in Section 5.1). The guarantees degrade gracefully with the prediction error.

The paper is exceptionally well-written and clear. Table 1 provides an excellent and concise roadmap of the results, and the intuitive explanations behind the certificates in Algorithm 1 and the tracking in Algorithm 2 are helpful.

Many positive bounds are accompanied by matching, tight impossibility results (such as the tight golden-ratio EFX approximation for identical valuations with normalization, and the zero-approximation impossibilities for EF1 with n >= 3).
weaknesses: Whether an EF1 allocation exists for n >= 3 under frequency predictions remains an unresolved open problem. While the authors explicitly state this as an open question and conjecture that it is impossible, resolving this would have fully completed the landscape in Table 1.

The assumption of an adaptive, adversarial arrival order for the frequency prediction model represents a very pessimistic worst-case view. In many ML contexts, the arrival order itself might be stochastic or show partial patterns; discussing how a more benign arrival process impacts the guarantees would be a valuable addition.

strengths: Comprehensive and Systematic Study: The paper provides a highly thorough mapping of the tractability of online fair division (EF1, EFX, PROP1, MMS) under three distinct information regimes, summarized beautifully in Table 1.

Strong Conceptual Contributions: The introduction of the 'frequency predictions' model and the meta-algorithm (Theorem 5.1) that translates offline share-based guarantees into online guarantees is highly elegant and widely applicable.

Rigorous Technical Depth: The proofs are mathematically rigorous, self-contained, and complete. The tight characterizations (e.g., the golden ratio approximation of EFX under identical valuations) demonstrate excellent technical execution.

Bridges Theory and ML: The inclusion of learning-augmented analyses under noisy predictions (with guarantees degrading gracefully with prediction error) connects classic fair division with modern predictive frameworks.
Outstanding Presentation: The writing is clear, the motivations are well-founded, and the exposition of certificate-based tracking is highly intuitive.
weaknesses: Restricted to Additive Valuations: While additivity is standard, the positive results rely heavily on this assumption, and extending them to broader classes (like submodular valuations) remains an open challenge.

Lack of Empirical Validation: Although the paper is primarily theoretical, a small simulation on synthetic or proxy dataset workloads showing how the algorithms behave and degrade under varying prediction noise would enhance its practical significance.

Acquisition of Frequency Predictions: While mathematically sound, obtaining detailed value multisets as advice in highly dynamic, real-world sequential environments might be operationally challenging.
